screens.title: The Project's Big Picture: Understanding Requirements and Scope
screens.narratorSegment: Before you start implementing features, you must understand why the project exists and what value it should deliver. This screen introduces the central idea: working without the project's big picture risks elegant solutions to the wrong problems. I will show concrete ways to discover the true needs—asking why, observing users, and validating assumptions with rapid prototypes—so your team builds what matters. We will also preview how user stories and acceptance criteria capture functional requirements, and why non-functional requirements like performance and security are equally decisive for architecture. Finally, you'll see how pragmatic change management keeps scope under control. As you move through the lesson, keep one question in mind: what problem are we actually solving for our users? That question will guide every interview, every story, and every decision about what to build now versus later.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › The Project's Big Picture
The Project's Big Picture
Understand value, users, and scope before building.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson
Discover, elicit, document, and control scope with pragmatic patterns.
Coming up
User stories, acceptance criteria, NFRs, and scope management.
Why this matters

Starting without the big picture is like building a house without blueprints. The work may look impressive but fail to house the real need. This lesson emphasizes the value of early discovery—asking why, observing users, and building quick prototypes—to align team decisions with business outcomes. A shared vision reduces rework and keeps the product focused on measurable benefits.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives define practical skills you will use on real projects. First, you'll learn to articulate the project's big picture—its business context and the user problems it should solve—so you can demonstrate why a feature matters. Second, you'll practice eliciting and documenting requirements using techniques like interviews, observation, and user stories with acceptance criteria. Third, you'll learn to identify and mitigate common pitfalls such as ambiguity, incomplete requirements, and scope creep so you can protect the team's time and focus. Fourth, you'll distinguish functional requirements, which define behavior, from non-functional requirements, which define measurable qualities like performance or security, and learn to make them testable. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify mastery by applying the skill to a small project. Think of these objectives as the map for the lesson: they guide discovery, documentation, and disciplined change so your team builds useful, sustainable software.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied
screens.narratorSegment: Now we translate objectives into practical steps you can execute on a team. For articulating the big picture, you'll practice summarizing the project's goal in one sentence and name two measurable outcomes. For elicitation, you'll run a short user interview checklist, combine it with observation, and produce at least one prototype or mock-up. For documentation, you will write user stories with three acceptance criteria each so engineers and testers share the same definition of done. For scope control, you'll role-play a stakeholder request and follow a change management checklist to show impacts on time and budget. These applied activities turn abstract learning targets into verifiable milestones. Each practice closes the gap between theory and delivery, so your team can start with “good enough” requirements and iterate toward clarity without freezing progress.

screens.title: Why the 'Big Picture' Matters
screens.narratorSegment: When we say 'big picture' we mean an agreed understanding of who benefits from the product, what problem is solved, and the measurable outcome that defines success. This is not a long, locked document; it is a shared hypothesis that guides decisions. A clear big picture prevents two common failures: teams building technically correct features that don't deliver value, and endless rework because the original problem was misunderstood. For example, a team writing an advanced search algorithm for a product might miss that users actually want faster discovery via curated lists; without discovery and user observation, the team optimizes the wrong metric. A practical approach is to craft a one-sentence goal and two measurable outcomes—such as reducing time-to-find by 30%—and validate those assumptions by watching users complete real tasks and by creating low-fidelity prototypes. A common misconception is that a detailed spec equals understanding; in reality, over-specification early can slow learning. The takeaway is to use the big picture as a living guide: concise, testable, and shared with stakeholders so you can align trade-offs and keep the project on course.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Why the 'Big Picture' Matters
Definition

The big picture is a concise, shared statement of who we serve, the problem to solve, and how success is measured.

One-sentence goal
Two measurable outcomes
Observation & prototype validation
Key Takeaway

Keep the big picture concise and testable so it guides priorities and reduces costly rework.

Concrete Example
A team thinks the problem is slow search. After observing users, they discover users instead struggle to discover new items. The new goal becomes increasing discovery events by 25 percent. A prototype of curated lists reveals faster success and avoids costly full-text indexing work.
Common misconception
Mistake: Treating a long spec as understanding. Reality: Specs become obsolete without discovery and validation.
Try this
Write one-sentence goal and two measurable outcomes. Run a 30-minute observation session to test the hypothesis.

screens.title: Requirements Elicitation Techniques
screens.narratorSegment: Eliciting requirements means uncovering needs and constraints that stakeholders may not state directly. Effective techniques include active listening, open-ended interviews, contextual inquiry (observing people in their environment), prototyping, and teach-back confirmation. Active listening surfaces hidden assumptions; open questions invite stories about actual work and pain points. Observing users reveals workflow shortcuts and friction that interviews alone might miss. Low-fidelity prototypes or mock-ups let stakeholders interact with proposed flows and provide concrete feedback early. A typical process looks like this: formulate a hypothesis about the user's problem, run an interview and observation session, create a quick prototype that addresses the hypothesis, then validate the prototype with users and iterate. A common pitfall is treating a stakeholder's suggested solution as a requirement; instead, record it as a proposal and test whether it solves the underlying need. By combining these techniques, you convert vague requests into testable, prioritized requirements that the team can implement with confidence. Requirements Elicitation Techniques means combine interviews, observation, and rapid prototyping to reveal true user needs and validate proposed solutions.. In practical terms, how to discover stakeholder needs beyond stated solutions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Combine interviews, observation, and rapid prototyping to reveal true user needs and validate proposed solutions.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Elicitation Techniques
Step-by-step elicitation
  1. Form a hypothesis about the user's problem or goal.
  2. Interview with open-ended questions; practice active listening.
  3. Observe the user in context to see actual workflows and friction.
  4. Build a low-fidelity prototype to test assumptions quickly.
  5. Use teach-back: ask the stakeholder to describe the solution in their words.
Key Takeaway

Elicitation is an iterative learning cycle: hypothesize, observe, prototype, validate.

Techniques & examples
Active listening — repeat and summarize stakeholder statements to expose assumptions.
Contextual inquiry — watch a user prepare an order to find hidden steps.
Prototype — a paper mock of checkout reveals missing edge cases.
Misconception
Mistake: Treating the stakeholder’s requested UI as the requirement. Contrast: test whether that UI actually solves the underlying task.

screens.title: Documenting Requirements: User Stories & Acceptance Criteria
screens.narratorSegment: User stories are a concise format that keeps focus on who benefits, what they want, and why it matters. The canonical template is: 'As a [type of user], I want to [perform some action] so that [I can achieve some goal].' Each story should be paired with acceptance criteria—clear, testable statements that define what 'done' means. Acceptance criteria turn vague expectations into verifiable conditions for developers and testers. For example, a shopping cart story may include criteria that the cart allows multiple instances of the same item and updates the total price when items are removed. A pragmatic approach keeps stories small enough to be implemented in an iteration and accepts that stories will be refined as more is learned. Avoid writing acceptance criteria as implementation steps; instead, state observable outcomes. A common mistake is overlong prose that buries the actual conditions. The goal is clarity: a short story plus three to five measurable acceptance criteria gives the team enough information to implement and verify functionality without creating brittle, outdated documentation. Documenting Requirements: User Stories & Acceptance Criteria means user stories plus measurable acceptance criteria create a concise, testable contract between stakeholders, developers, and testers.. In practical terms, capture actionable functional requirements that teams can implement and test. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › User Stories & Acceptance Criteria
User story format
As a [user], I want to [action] so that [benefit].
Keep stories focused on user goals, not the UI. Pair each story with acceptance criteria that are measurable and testable.
Common pitfall
Writing acceptance criteria as implementation steps instead of observable outcomes.
Concrete example
<!-- User Story example --> As a Customer, I want to add items to my shopping cart so that I can purchase multiple products at once. Acceptance Criteria: 1. The system allows adding multiple instances of the same item. 2. The cart displays the total price including item quantities. 3. Removing an item updates the total price immediately.
This concrete format provides enough detail for developers to implement features and for testers to verify correctness without a huge, brittle specification.
Key Takeaway

Write short stories and clear, measurable acceptance criteria to create testable requirements.

screens.title: User Story & Acceptance Criteria Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a simple e-commerce user story and its acceptance criteria so you can see how this structure guides development and testing. The story reads: 'As a Customer, I want to add items to my shopping cart so that I can purchase multiple products at once.' Acceptance criteria should be written as observable outcomes, not implementation steps. For this story, criteria include allowing multiple instances of the same item, displaying an accurate total price, and updating the total when an item is removed. In practice, developers will use these criteria to write unit and integration tests, while testers will validate each criterion against the running application. A common misconception is that acceptance criteria must specify UI details; instead, focus on behavior and results. If the team needs UI specifics, add them in a separate design note but keep acceptance criteria platform-agnostic. Use this pattern when you convert stakeholder requests into developer-ready work items and ask: can I write a test that proves this criterion? If yes, the criterion is clear. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › User Story Walkthrough
User Story
As a Customer, I want to add items to my shopping cart so that I can purchase multiple products at once.
Acceptance Criteria (behavior-focused)
1. The system allows adding multiple instances of the same item.
2. The shopping cart displays the correct total price including item quantities.
3. Removing an item updates the total price immediately and persistently.
4. If no items exist, the cart shows an empty state message.
These criteria are directly testable. Each line should map to an automated or manual test. Keep criteria concise and avoid describing how the UI must be implemented.
Why this helps
  • Developers implement to observable behavior, not guessed UI steps.
  • Testers verify acceptance criteria directly against outcomes.
  • Stakeholders see clear evidence of completion.
Misconception
Avoid writing acceptance criteria as a checklist of UI clicks. Focus on what must be true when the feature works.
Key Takeaway

Translate stories into measurable criteria that drive implementation and testing, keeping UI details separate when not essential.

screens.title: Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements
screens.narratorSegment: A critical distinction in requirements is between functional requirements, which describe specific behaviors or features, and non-functional requirements, which describe measurable qualities of the system. Functional requirements answer 'what' the system does: login, search, add to cart. Non-functional requirements answer 'how well' it does those things: performance, security, scalability, reliability, and maintainability. Non-functional requirements often have the largest architectural impact. For example, the statement 'the product page should load instantly' is not a functional feature but a performance requirement that must be quantified—what does 'instantly' mean? A pragmatic next step is to convert such statements into measurable targets, like response time under two seconds for 95 percent of requests. A common mistake is to overlook NFRs or leave them informal; that leads to late surprises when the chosen architecture cannot meet expectations. Always capture NFRs as testable metrics and consider them during design, not as afterthoughts. Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements means functional: behavior. non-functional: measurable qualities that shape architecture and testing.. In practical terms, what the system does versus how it performs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Functional vs Non-Functional
Functional Requirements
  • Describe what the system does: features and behaviors.
  • Example: Add item to cart, process payment, search products.
  • Captured with user stories and acceptance criteria.
Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs)
  • Describe how the system performs: speed, security, reliability, scalability.
  • Example measurable NFR: "Respond within 2 seconds 95% of the time."
  • NFRs drive architecture decisions and testing strategies.
Misconception
Assuming functionality alone is enough. In practice, poor non-functional qualities make a system unusable despite feature completeness.
Key Takeaway

Specify NFRs in measurable terms early; they shape architecture and must be tested just like functional requirements.

screens.title: How NFRs Influence System Design
screens.narratorSegment: Non-functional requirements are often the primary drivers of architecture. A performance target, security requirement, or scalability expectation forces concrete design choices. For example, a strict latency requirement might require caching, CDN integration, or a change in data model. A security requirement might mandate authentication, encryption, and stricter access controls that influence service boundaries. Maintainability and operability concerns affect how code is organized, how monitoring is structured, and how deployments are automated. The pragmatic approach is to record NFRs as measurable constraints early and consider them when selecting components and trade-offs. One misconception is that NFRs can be bolted on later. In practice this leads to expensive rewrites. Instead, evaluate each major design option against your NFR checklist during architecture reviews. Ask: will this option meet the specified metrics? If not, either refine the NFRs or choose a different design. Document the rationale so future teams understand why certain trade-offs were made. How NFRs Influence System Design means treat measurable non-functional requirements as constraints that directly shape architecture and trade-offs.. In practical terms, from performance targets to maintainability trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › NFRs and Architecture
NFR examples and architectural impacts
Performance target: adds caching layer, database tuning, CDN
Security: enforces authentication, encryption, access control
Scalability: triggers stateless service design and horizontal scaling
Pragmatic checklist
  1. Record NFRs as measurable targets.
  2. Evaluate architecture options against NFR metrics.
  3. Document trade-offs and revisit them when requirements change.
Misconception
Treating NFRs as optional details. In reality, they constrain choices and must be planned early.
Key Takeaway

Make NFRs explicit and measurable, then use them as criteria in architecture decisions.

screens.title: Managing Scope Creep
screens.narratorSegment: Scope creep arises when features or requirements are added without adjusting time, budget, or priorities. It usually starts as small requests that accumulate until the project drifts off course. The pragmatic response combines clear communication, a simple change management process, and an emphasis on prioritization. Each new request should be documented, evaluated for impact on the project's core objectives, and prioritized against existing work. If a request is essential, explicitly record the trade-offs: how much schedule or budget must change, and who approves it. A common, effective tactic is a courteous conversation with the stakeholder that explains the process and why it protects delivery. Another safe pattern is adding non-urgent requests to a backlog and scheduling them for a future iteration, rather than implementing them ad hoc. This transparency prevents hidden expansion of scope and helps maintain stakeholder trust. Regularly reviewing the project's vision with stakeholders keeps everyone aligned about what will be delivered in the current iteration. Managing Scope Creep means use transparent evaluation and change approval to prevent informal requests from derailing the project.. In practical terms, evaluate requests and keep the project focused. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Change evaluation process
Document the request with rationale and stakeholder.
Assess impact on schedule, budget, and scope.
Decide: approve, defer to backlog, or reject with explanation.

A simple, visible change process preserves focus and prevents cumulative feature expansion.

Practical tips
  • Say "not now" with a reason and add the request to a prioritized backlog.

A marketing ask to add a promotional carousel arrives mid-sprint. Log it, estimate impact, and either schedule for the next sprint or get approval for scope change now.

screens.title: Prioritization and Iterative Refinement

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Prioritization & Iteration
Priority matrix
High value, low risk — implement
High value, high risk — prototype first
Low value, low risk — schedule later
Low value, high cost — avoid
Iteration patterns
  • Deliver minimal increments that provide user value.
  • Reserve time for experiments and prototypes to reduce risk.
  • Revisit acceptance criteria after user feedback and adjust priorities.
Misconception
Mistake: Equating iteration with chaos. In fact, iteration demands measured experiments and clear acceptance criteria.
Key Takeaway

Break work into small, testable increments and use feedback to refine requirements rather than perfecting them upfront.

screens.title: Common Pitfalls in Requirements Gathering
screens.narratorSegment: Requirements work is vulnerable to several recurring mistakes. Teams often assume they know what stakeholders mean, leading to ambiguous or incorrect requirements. Another frequent error is failing to involve the right people—excluding a user group or operations staff can hide crucial constraints. Over-documenting requirements in heavy, formal documents leads to stale, unread material that doesn't help daily decisions. Conversely, under-documenting leaves too much to memory. Analysis paralysis is also common: teams try to perfect requirements before starting, delaying learning. The pragmatic alternatives are teach-back confirmation, short prototypes, and living documentation—concise notes that evolve with the product. Teach-back means restating the requirement in your words and asking the stakeholder to confirm; this quickly reveals misunderstandings. The key is balance: capture enough detail to start safely, validate quickly, and iterate. Spotting these pitfalls early preserves budget and schedule and improves final product fit. Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Activity: Recipe App
Activity steps
  1. Identify 3 user types: Home Cook, Professional Chef, Dietary Planner.
  2. For each user, list two features (eg. add recipe, search, categorize).
  3. Write user stories in the "As a..., I want..., so that..." format.
  4. Define at least 3 acceptance criteria per story and perform teach-back.
Example starter for Home Cook
// User Story
As a Home Cook, I want to add a new recipe to my collection so that I can easily find and use it later.

Acceptance Criteria:
1. The system allows input of recipe name, ingredients, and instructions.
2. The recipe name must be non-empty before saving.
3. The user may optionally upload an image and the save redirects to the recipe detail page.
Use this example as a template for other user types and features. After drafting, role-play the stakeholder to validate each story’s assumptions.

fullNarratorScript:
Before you start implementing features, you must understand why the project exists and what value it should deliver. This screen introduces the central idea: working without the project's big picture risks elegant solutions to the wrong problems. I will show concrete ways to discover the true needs—asking why, observing users, and validating assumptions with rapid prototypes—so your team builds what matters. We will also preview how user stories and acceptance criteria capture functional requirements, and why non-functional requirements like performance and security are equally decisive for architecture. Finally, you'll see how pragmatic change management keeps scope under control. As you move through the lesson, keep one question in mind: what problem are we actually solving for our users? That question will guide every interview, every story, and every decision about what to build now versus later.

These objectives define practical skills you will use on real projects. First, you'll learn to articulate the project's big picture—its business context and the user problems it should solve—so you can demonstrate why a feature matters. Second, you'll practice eliciting and documenting requirements using techniques like interviews, observation, and user stories with acceptance criteria. Third, you'll learn to identify and mitigate common pitfalls such as ambiguity, incomplete requirements, and scope creep so you can protect the team's time and focus. Fourth, you'll distinguish functional requirements, which define behavior, from non-functional requirements, which define measurable qualities like performance or security, and learn to make them testable. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify mastery by applying the skill to a small project. Think of these objectives as the map for the lesson: they guide discovery, documentation, and disciplined change so your team builds useful, sustainable software.

Now we translate objectives into practical steps you can execute on a team. For articulating the big picture, you'll practice summarizing the project's goal in one sentence and name two measurable outcomes. For elicitation, you'll run a short user interview checklist, combine it with observation, and produce at least one prototype or mock-up. For documentation, you will write user stories with three acceptance criteria each so engineers and testers share the same definition of done. For scope control, you'll role-play a stakeholder request and follow a change management checklist to show impacts on time and budget. These applied activities turn abstract learning targets into verifiable milestones. Each practice closes the gap between theory and delivery, so your team can start with “good enough” requirements and iterate toward clarity without freezing progress.

When we say 'big picture' we mean an agreed understanding of who benefits from the product, what problem is solved, and the measurable outcome that defines success. This is not a long, locked document; it is a shared hypothesis that guides decisions. A clear big picture prevents two common failures: teams building technically correct features that don't deliver value, and endless rework because the original problem was misunderstood. For example, a team writing an advanced search algorithm for a product might miss that users actually want faster discovery via curated lists; without discovery and user observation, the team optimizes the wrong metric. A practical approach is to craft a one-sentence goal and two measurable outcomes—such as reducing time-to-find by 30%—and validate those assumptions by watching users complete real tasks and by creating low-fidelity prototypes. A common misconception is that a detailed spec equals understanding; in reality, over-specification early can slow learning. The takeaway is to use the big picture as a living guide: concise, testable, and shared with stakeholders so you can align trade-offs and keep the project on course.

Eliciting requirements means uncovering needs and constraints that stakeholders may not state directly. Effective techniques include active listening, open-ended interviews, contextual inquiry (observing people in their environment), prototyping, and teach-back confirmation. Active listening surfaces hidden assumptions; open questions invite stories about actual work and pain points. Observing users reveals workflow shortcuts and friction that interviews alone might miss. Low-fidelity prototypes or mock-ups let stakeholders interact with proposed flows and provide concrete feedback early. A typical process looks like this: formulate a hypothesis about the user's problem, run an interview and observation session, create a quick prototype that addresses the hypothesis, then validate the prototype with users and iterate. A common pitfall is treating a stakeholder's suggested solution as a requirement; instead, record it as a proposal and test whether it solves the underlying need. By combining these techniques, you convert vague requests into testable, prioritized requirements that the team can implement with confidence. User stories are a concise format that keeps focus on who benefits, what they want, and why it matters. The canonical template is: 'As a [type of user], I want to [perform some action] so that [I can achieve some goal].' Each story should be paired with acceptance criteria—clear, testable statements that define what 'done' means. Acceptance criteria turn vague expectations into verifiable conditions for developers and testers. For example, a shopping cart story may include criteria that the cart allows multiple instances of the same item and updates the total price when items are removed. A pragmatic approach keeps stories small enough to be implemented in an iteration and accepts that stories will be refined as more is learned. Avoid writing acceptance criteria as implementation steps; instead, state observable outcomes. A common mistake is overlong prose that buries the actual conditions. The goal is clarity: a short story plus three to five measurable acceptance criteria gives the team enough information to implement and verify functionality without creating brittle, outdated documentation. Let's walk through a simple e-commerce user story and its acceptance criteria so you can see how this structure guides development and testing. The story reads: 'As a Customer, I want to add items to my shopping cart so that I can purchase multiple products at once.' Acceptance criteria should be written as observable outcomes, not implementation steps. For this story, criteria include allowing multiple instances of the same item, displaying an accurate total price, and updating the total when an item is removed. In practice, developers will use these criteria to write unit and integration tests, while testers will validate each criterion against the running application. A critical distinction in requirements is between functional requirements, which describe specific behaviors or features, and non-functional requirements, which describe measurable qualities of the system. Functional requirements answer 'what' the system does: login, search, add to cart. Non-functional requirements answer 'how well' it does those things: performance, security, scalability, reliability, and maintainability. Non-functional requirements often have the largest architectural impact. For example, the statement 'the product page should load instantly' is not a functional feature but a performance requirement that must be quantified—what does 'instantly' mean? A pragmatic next step is to convert such statements into measurable targets, like response time under two seconds for 95 percent of requests. Non-functional requirements are often the primary drivers of architecture. A performance target, security requirement, or scalability expectation forces concrete design choices. For example, a strict latency requirement might require caching, CDN integration, or a change in data model. These three core concepts summarize the chapter. First, the Big Picture: always capture who benefits, the problem, and measurable outcomes before committing major effort. Second, Requirements Elicitation: use interviews, observation, prototypes, and teach-back to discover true needs rather than accepting suggested solutions at face value. Third, User Stories and Acceptance Criteria: write short, user-focused stories with clear, testable acceptance criteria so developers and testers have a shared definition of done. Internalize these concepts and use them as guiding principles each time you begin a project. They reduce wasted work and make requirements actionable and verifiable. Three more essential concepts complete the chapter's memory set. First, Non-Functional Requirements: specify measurable qualities like performance and security and treat them as architecture constraints. Second, Scope Creep and Change Management: require transparent evaluation and approval of changes to protect time and budget. Third, Iterative Refinement: prefer starting with good-enough requirements, deliver small increments, and learn from feedback to refine requirements. Together these concepts ensure requirements are not only correct but achievable and resilient to change. Keep this set as a checklist during planning and architecture discussions.
